A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, and their complete main texts, equations, tables and appendices support comparison. Relocated material is identifiable: v1's Deep Sets appendix E becomes v2's appendix D, and technical lemmas move from D to G.

before.justification: v1 reports theoretical constructions, bounds and proofs, but no original empirical outcomes. Its discussion of PoolFormer experiments attributes those results to Yu et al.

after.justification: Appendix H reports original training and memorization experiments on MultiNLI, IMDb and synthetic data, including Figures 1–3.

M1.justification: The original uniform-attention construction is retained. Appendix F adds a limited-precision adaptation that partitions examples into groups of B², composes subnetworks with an accumulator, and substitutes these into the two feed-forward components. This yields an additional width-15 construction alongside the original width-14 result.

E1.justification: v1 has no empirical dataset coverage. v2 introduces sequence-label memorization experiments using sampled MultiNLI and IMDb data, plus synthetic sequences of six-dimensional uniform-random tokens with random binary labels.

E2.justification: Neither version empirically evaluates competing baseline methods. Appendix H compares depth configurations of the same uniform-attention architecture. Table 1 retains the same literature comparison methods.

E3.justification: Appendix H introduces experimental protocols absent from v1: minimum block count as a capacity proxy, cross-entropy and mean-squared-error objectives, a training-error threshold of 0.01, and controlled dataset-size and sequence-length sweeps. Figures 1–3 specify 1000 training epochs and selection from two or ten Optuna tuning trials.

E4.justification: v2 adds depth sensitivity experiments on MultiNLI and IMDb, a MultiNLI dataset-size sweep from 600 to 1700 examples, and a synthetic sequence-length sweep from 10 to 10000 tokens at N=500. These examine uniform-attention memorization and capacity scaling; v1 contains no corresponding empirical analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent replication counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v2's two- and ten-trial Optuna counts describe hyperparameter search budgets and best-model selection, rather than replication-based uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds training-loss and accuracy curves in Figures 1–2 and capacity measurements in Figure 3. The latter rises from five blocks at N=1400 to sixteen at N=1700. The synthetic experiment reports four blocks as the smallest successful model for every tested sequence length. These are new outcomes, with no empirical counterparts in v1.

T1.justification: Appendix E adds a theorem and construction for embedding layers, expanding v1's brief remark. Appendix F adds proofs of a parameter–precision tradeoff: O-tilde(N^(1-epsilon)) parameters with O-tilde(N^epsilon) bits per parameter. v2 also corrects cross-sequence indexing in Assumption 4.1, reformulates Theorem 4.2 around shattering repeated-token sequences, and revises supporting bounds, including N^4 to N^5 in Theorem B.1's R.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central near-optimal square-root parameter bounds, negligible sequence-length dependence for next-token prediction, the hardmax qualification for sequence-to-sequence optimality, and the feed-forward bottleneck interpretation. The added material does not redefine these main claims.

C2.justification: Appendix H adds a proposed finite-precision explanation for the capacity increase beyond N=1400 and interprets the synthetic results as suggesting nearly sequence-length-independent capacity. These supplement the retained mechanism explanations and softmax open problem; the precision explanation is presented as plausible rather than experimentally isolated.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the experimental architecture with embedding dimension 2 and hidden dimension 4m, AdamW with full-batch updates, learning-rate and warmup tuning, sequence truncation and output-token selection, and synthetic input and label distributions. v1 contains no corresponding experimental implementation information.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for Optuna, AdamW, IMDb, GLUE and MultiNLI, and explicitly connects the limited-precision extension to Vardi et al.'s construction. The main related-work discussion and literature comparator membership remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. v2 modifies the title, expands selected proof explanations and notation entries, adds acknowledgments and cross-references, and reorganizes existing appendices around the new extensions and experiments. This is localized editing rather than a broad narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds three figures containing five plots of training behavior and memorization capacity. Table 1 replaces its binary single-layer column with explicit layer-complexity entries and is reformatted. The paper also adopts the ICLR conference layout, changing typography, headings, spacing and running headers throughout.

improvement.justification: The strongest gains are theoretical: Appendix E substantiates the earlier embedding-layer remark, while Appendix F derives a precision–parameter tradeoff beyond the original construction. Corrections to assumptions and bounds improve consistency, and Appendix H provides the first direct empirical checks. The empirical scaling claims remain suggestive because best-tuned runs lack uncertainty estimates and do not isolate precision effects. These limitations temper the experimental contribution but do not outweigh the substantial gains in theoretical completeness and applicability.
